newsitem.title: UK: Tajik rebel leader said to have agreed to talks.
newsitem.headline: Tajik rebel leader said to have agreed to talks.

text.p: Tajik rebel leader Makhmud Khudoyberdyev has announced the withdrawal of his forces from some areas and agreed to talks with Tajikistan authorities, Russia's Itar-Tass news agency said in a report monitored by the BBC on Wednesday.

"Khudoyberdyev has announced that his force withdraws from fighting on the Fakhrobad pass and in other areas. He has issued a statement of consent to meet delegates of the Tajik leadership for talks at any time and place," the agency said.

It quoted one of Khudoyberdyev's advisers as saying the rebel leader had taken the decision in order to avoid further casualties and because the proximity of a fertiliser factory meant an explosion could cause a serious environmental disaster.
No independent confirmation of the report was immediately available.
Another agency, Interfax, also monitored by the BBC, said Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and Khudoyberdyev, a mutinous colonel, spoke by telephone on Tuesday night.
"Rakhmonov called for an immediate ceasefire," the agency said, quoting an unidentified source.
Interfax said a Tajik government delegation was expected to fly from Dushanbe on Wednesday to hold talks with the rebel leaders.
The front line between the two sides was quiet, it added.
Burning fields saw Tajikistan's hard won peace go up in smoke on Tuesday as government forces in the former Soviet republic rocketed positions held by Khudoyberdyev south of the capital Dushanbe.
Clouds of acrid brown smoke hung over the Fakhrobad valley as the presidential guard, loyal to Rakhmonov, unleashed Grad rockets against troops fighting for the renegade colonel.
There have been no reliable casualty figures, although the International Committee of the Red Cross said at the weekend it had provided medicine for 40 wounded in Dushanbe.

The eruption of fighting on Saturday is not linked to the republic's armed Islamic opposition, with whom the government signed a peace accord in June aimed at ending four years of civil war. That conflict claimed tens of thousands of lives.
The latest clashes show Rakhmonov's grip on power as tenuous as ever and the impoverished republic far from the peace craved by its 5.7 million population.
Khudoyberdyev, 34, the commander of an elite government armoured brigade, has mutinied twice before in as many years.
He moved his armour towards Dushanbe at the weekend in the wake of fighting between two rival warlords in the capital.
The renegade colonel has not revealed his motives but he is counted by western diplomats as a potential coup maker.

"I'm not trying to move on Dushanbe," Khudoyberdyev told Reuters by telephone on Tuesday. "Government forces provoked us by moving toward Kurgan Tyube (his headquarters) -- we had to defend ourselves".
On Sunday, Rakhmonov issued a three-day ultimatum to Khudoyberdyev to lay down his arms or face "destruction".
Gun law has seen Tajikistan divided up into a complicated patchwork of independent fiefdoms under the control of armed groups like those in neighbouring Afghanistan.
Khudoyberdyev said aircraft had bombed Kalininabad, a town near his base about 120 km (80 miles) south of Dushanbe.
He lost control of a strategically important aluminium smelter west of the capital to the presidential guard on Monday.
Russia, which deploys 20,000 troops in the Central Asian state and which fears unrest along its unstable southern rim, has been cautious in its reaction to the fighting.
On Tuesday, the predominantly Russian peacekeeping force in Tajikistan fielded by the Commonwealth of Independent States said it would stay neutral and take no part in the conflict.
